body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students describe how the manor, feudal obligations, the Church and guilds shaped people's lives (D2.Civ.6.6-8), and determine the meaning of domain words such as vassal, fief and serf (RH.6-8.4).
- Students examine the origins, purposes and impact of Magna Carta (D2.Civ.3.6-8) and connect it to broader developments in law and government (D2.His.1.6-8), citing evidence from the text (RH.6-8.1).
- Students explain multiple causes and effects of the Black Death (D2.His.14.6-8) with well-chosen facts and details (WHST.6-8.2.B).
- Students evaluate the relative influence of two developments on ordinary people and support a claim with logical reasoning and evidence (D2.His.15.6-8, D2.His.16.6-8, WHST.6-8.1.B).

MATERIALS
- Lords, Vassals and the Manor (lesson reading)
- Magna Carta, 1215 (selected clauses)
- The Great Mortality (reading)
- A diagram of a manor (village, fields in strips, mill, church, manor house, common land)
- A role-card set: king, noble, knight, priest, serf, guild member

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read the overview. Role-card simulation: each student draws a card and learns what they owe and are owed; the class builds a web of obligations on the board. Discuss why historians debate the word feudalism. Begin the lesson, Lords, Vassals and the Manor.
Day 2: Finish the lesson. Introduce King John and the barons' grievances. Read Magna Carta's clauses 12, 39 and 40 aloud, paraphrasing each together. Students begin Magna Carta, 1215.
Day 3: Finish Magna Carta, 1215. Discussion: in 1215, who counted as a "free man"? How did later generations use clause 39?
Day 4: Read The Great Mortality. Students complete The Great Mortality cause-and-effect explanation. Note sensitively that some communities were falsely blamed and attacked, and why scapegoating happens.
Day 5: Assessment: Which Changed More?

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: provide a labeled manor diagram and a vocabulary card set (vassal, fief, serf, tithe, guild). Offer a clause-paraphrase table with the first one done.
- Support: give a cause-and-effect chain for the Black Death with the first and last boxes filled in.
- Stretch: research how clause 39 was later used in English law and how its ideas appear in the Fifth Amendment of the United States Constitution ("due process of law").
- Multilingual learners: use pictures for each social role; pre-teach the legal words arrested, imprisoned, exiled and judgment; allow students to paraphrase each clause first in their home language, then in English.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This unit we are studying Europe in the Middle Ages: knights and castles, but also the farmers who did most of the work, the Church, the famous charter called Magna Carta (1215), and the Black Death of 1347. Magna Carta said that no free man could be imprisoned or have his property taken except by lawful judgment or the law of the land, an idea that later shaped the United States Constitution. Ask your child: in 1215, who did Magna Carta protect, and who did it leave out?
title: Teacher guide: Medieval Europe
